paragraphs.text: Desmin-related myopathy is a familial skeletal muscle weakness that occurs with cardiac conduction blocks, arrhythmias, and restrictive heart failure. In both cardiac and skeletal muscle cells, desmin-reactive deposits build up inside the cytoplasm (Goldfarb et al., 1998). The clinical picture varies. It includes myopathies, cardiomyopathies, conduction disease, and combinations of these (van Tintelen et al., 2009). In a meta-analysis of 159 DES mutation carriers, van Spaendonck-Zwarts et al. (2011) found that symptoms usually began in the 30s. Atrioventricular block was an important hallmark, and most mutations were dominant.

paragraphs.text: Myofibrillar myopathy (MFM) is defined by its pathology. Myofibrils dissolve, the breakdown products accumulate, and multiple proteins are expressed ectopically, including desmin, alpha-B-crystallin, and dystrophin, along with congophilic amyloid material. MFM is genetically heterogeneous (Selcen et al., 2004).

paragraphs.text: Porte et al. (1980) reported 3 brothers with progressive myocardial deficiency. On histology, most cardiac muscle cells held massive stores of PAS-negative proteinaceous material. On electron microscopy, this material consisted of sinuous filaments 7 to 10 nm in diameter, similar to the intermediate filaments normally found in cardiac muscle cells. Where filaments were stored, the neighboring myofibrils were disintegrating, with Z-band changes that formed rod-like bodies and more complex structures. These changes were associated with extensive development and involution of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, together with relatively high glycogen accumulation. A few skeletal muscle fibers showed sarcoplasmic reticulum proliferation, glycogen overload, and filament deposits. The authors suggested that a disturbance in desmin metabolism might be involved. Stoeckel et al. (1981) further described this unusual familial cardiomyopathy as having aberrant accumulations of desmin-type intermediate filaments.

One patient also had congenital paresis of the pupillary dilator muscle and cardiomyopathy. paragraphs.text: Abe et al. (1993) described a Japanese kindred with autosomal dominant progressive myopathy with diffuse cytoplasmic bodies. Over 4 successive generations, 12 patients had weakness and atrophy of muscles of the distal extremities, neck, thorax, and shoulder girdles. Mean age at onset was 42 years, and patients became disabled 5 to 10 years later from chronic respiratory failure. Serum creatine kinase was normal or slightly elevated. Electromyography showed mainly myopathic changes with slight neurogenic changes. Autopsy in 2 cases showed numerous cytoplasmic bodies in skeletal muscle, mostly in type I fibers, and smooth and cardiac muscle were also affected. Males were affected more often than females (2:1).

paragraphs.text: Horowitz and Schmalbruch (1994) described a large family with autosomal dominant distal myopathy. Onset was in early to middle adulthood, with gait disturbance from distal leg weakness. Over 5 to 10 years the disease spread to all extremities and to bulbar, respiratory, and facial muscles. Cardiac involvement was frequent, with arrhythmias, conduction blocks, and congestive failure, and led to premature death. Electromyography showed prominent spontaneous activity, short-duration motor unit potentials, and polyphasia. Muscle biopsies from multiple family members showed desmin storage and autophagocytosis.

paragraphs.text: Melberg et al. (1999) studied 21 members of a Swedish family with myopathy and cardiomyopathy and reviewed the records of 2 affected deceased patients. Twelve patients had myopathy. Weakness was axial in mildly affected patients, axial and mainly distal in moderately affected patients, and generalized in severely affected patients. Electromyography showed myopathic signs in 10 patients. Muscle biopsies showed myopathic changes, rimmed vacuoles, and accumulation of desmin, dystrophin, and other proteins. Electron microscopy showed granulofilamentous changes and disorganized myofibrils. Several patients had episodes of chest pain or palpitations. Three men had arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, with nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, atrial flutter, and ventricular dilatation affecting mainly the right ventricle. Two of them received pacemakers for atrioventricular block and sick sinus syndrome. Onset and severity of skeletal and cardiac involvement varied.

paragraphs.text: Selcen et al. (2004) reviewed 63 unrelated patients diagnosed with MFM at the Mayo Clinic between 1977 and 2003. Age at onset was 54 +/- 16 years (mean +/- SD). Weakness was both proximal and distal in 77% and proximal only in 13%, and 16% had cardiomyopathy. Electromyography showed a myopathic pattern with abnormal electrical irritability. In trichrome-stained sections, abnormal fibers contained amorphous, granular, or pleomorphic hyaline structures, which were strongly congophilic, and vacuoles with membranous material. Among abnormal fibers, an average of 90%, 75%, 75%, 70%, and 70% abnormally expressed myotilin, desmin, alpha-B-crystallin, dystrophin, and beta-amyloid precursor protein, respectively. Electron microscopy showed progressive myofibrillar degeneration beginning at the Z disk.

paragraphs.text: Pinol-Ripoll et al. (2009) reported a girl who was the only child of consanguineous parents (uncle and niece). She had recurrent syncope from 6 months of age, which was first attributed to Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome. From 3 years of age she had progressive syncopal, presyncopal, and cyanotic attacks. At 15 years, she had a long, narrow face with bilateral facial weakness, ptosis, symmetric scapular winging, and poor muscle bulk. She also had atrophy of the masseter, temporalis, sternocleidomastoid, and trunk muscles, bilateral pes cavus, mild weakness of the shoulder girdle and distal limb muscles, and hypoactive deep tendon reflexes. Creatine kinase was twice normal. Electromyography showed complex repetitive discharges, some myotonic discharges, and a myopathic recruitment pattern. Holter monitoring showed monomorphic and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, occasional QT prolongation, and second-degree AV block, and a defibrillator and pacemaker were implanted. At 18 years, she had several episodes of ventricular tachyarrhythmia. Echocardiography then showed mild left ventricular systolic dysfunction (LVEF 45%), slight right ventricular dilatation, markedly enlarged atria, and filling consistent with restrictive cardiomyopathy. Diarrhea, vomiting, and weight loss suggested involvement of intestinal smooth muscle. She died of cardiac failure before age 21. On muscle biopsy, more than 90% of fibers had subsarcolemmal deposits of eosinophilic, Congo red-positive material that was strongly desmin-immunoreactive. On electron microscopy, the deposits formed a granulofilamentous matrix. The authors described her as the youngest known patient with desminopathy.

checks.claim: Messina et al. (1997) reported a family with 6q23-linked limb-girdle muscular dystrophy 1D/1E.
checks.evidence_quote: We now characterize an autosomal dominant disorder involving dilated cardiomyopathy, cardiac conduction-system disease, and adult-onset limb-girdle muscular dystrophy
checks.explanation: The paper describes a 6q23-linked disorder that includes limb-girdle muscular dystrophy. The LGMD1D/1E names are not in the paper, and the abstract does not say a single family was studied.

checks.claim: Greenberg et al. (2012) identified the DES IVS3+3A-G mutation in a patient and family members with the 6q23-linked limb-girdle muscular dystrophy 1D/1E reported by Messina et al. (1997).
checks.evidence_quote: Sequencing in this patient and family members identified the genetic basis of the previously reported 6q23 linked LGMD1D/1E to be due to an intron splice donor site mutation (IVS3+3A>G) of the desmin gene
checks.explanation: The mutation in the patient and family members is stated, but the abstract does not name Messina et al. (1997).

checks.claim: Desmin was identified by laser capture microdissection proteomics as the main constituent of muscle inclusions in the limb-girdle muscular dystrophy 1D/1E patient.
checks.evidence_quote: We used laser capture microdissection to isolate cytoplasmic inclusions from skeletal muscle from a patient with LGMD1D/1E, performed mass spectrometry-based proteomics on these minute inclusions, and identified through bioinformatics desmin as their major constituent.
checks.explanation: The abstract says laser capture microdissection proteomics identified desmin as the main constituent of the inclusions.

paragraphs.text: In a patient with skeletal and cardiac myopathy, Park et al. (2000) found a G-to-A transition at the highly conserved -1 position of the intron 2 splice acceptor site of the DES gene (IVS2-1G-A). Expression of genomic fragments showed that the mutation caused deletion of exon 3.

checks.claim: Park et al. (2000) studied a patient with skeletal and cardiac myopathy.
checks.evidence_quote: was found in an unrelated patient with a similar phenotype
checks.explanation: The phenotype is described as similar to the skeletal and cardiac myopathy of the first patient.

checks.claim: Park et al. (2000) found a G-to-A transition at the -1 position of the intron 2 splice acceptor site of the DES gene (IVS2-1G-A) in a patient with skeletal and cardiac myopathy.
checks.evidence_quote: A G to A transition at the highly conserved -1 nucleotide position of intron 2 affecting the splice acceptor site (IVS2-1G-->A) was found in an unrelated patient with a similar phenotype.
checks.explanation: The variant matches the abstract, and the patient's phenotype is described as similar (skeletal and cardiac myopathy).

checks.claim: The -1 position of the DES intron 2 splice acceptor site is highly conserved.
checks.evidence_quote: A G to A transition at the highly conserved -1 nucleotide position of intron 2 affecting the splice acceptor site
checks.explanation: The abstract calls this position highly conserved.

checks.claim: Expression of genomic fragments showed that the DES IVS2-1G-A mutation caused deletion of exon 3.
checks.evidence_quote: Expression of genomic DNA fragments carrying the IVS3+3A-->G and IVS2-1G-->A mutations confirmed that these mutations cause exon 3 deletion.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this mutation causes exon 3 deletion.

paragraphs.text: Kaminska et al. (2004) identified an in-frame deletion, E359_S361del, in the DES gene in a family with skeletal or cardioskeletal myopathy. Structural analysis indicated that the deletion adds a second stutter immediately downstream of the natural stutter in the 2B coiled-coil segment. Expression studies showed that the mutant desmin could not polymerize into a functional filamentous network.

checks.claim: Kaminska et al. (2004) identified an in-frame deletion, E359_S361del, in the DES gene in a family with skeletal or cardioskeletal myopathy.
checks.evidence_quote: We have studied three families with skeletal or cardioskeletal myopathy caused by small in-frame deletions in the desmin gene. The newly identified in-frame deletions E359_S361del and N366del
checks.explanation: The deletion and the phenotypes are reported, but the abstract does not say which family carries E359_S361del or that it was found in one family.

checks.claim: Structural analysis indicated that the DES E359_S361del deletion adds a second stutter immediately downstream of the natural stutter in the 2B coiled-coil segment.
checks.evidence_quote: Structural analysis reveals that the E359_S361 deletion introduces a second stutter immediately downstream of the naturally occurring stutter
checks.explanation: Stated directly. The abstract places the deletions within the 2B segment, but it does not explicitly say the stutter lies in the 2B segment.

checks.claim: Expression studies showed that E359_S361del mutant desmin could not polymerize into a functional filamentous network.
checks.evidence_quote: Expression studies in two cell lines confirm the inability of desmin molecules with this changed architecture to polymerize into a functional filamentous network.
checks.explanation: Stated for the mutants as a group, which includes E359_S361del.

paragraphs.text: Kaminska et al. (2004) identified an in-frame deletion, N366del, in the DES gene in a family with skeletal or cardioskeletal myopathy. Structural analysis predicted that the deletion converts the wild-type stutter into a stammer. In 2 cell lines, the mutant desmin could not form a filamentous network.

checks.claim: Kaminska et al. (2004) identified an in-frame deletion, N366del, in the DES gene in a family with skeletal or cardioskeletal myopathy.
checks.evidence_quote: We have studied three families with skeletal or cardioskeletal myopathy caused by small in-frame deletions in the desmin gene. The newly identified in-frame deletions E359_S361del and N366del
checks.explanation: The deletion and the phenotypes are reported, but the abstract does not say which family carries N366del or that it was found in one family.

checks.claim: Structural analysis predicted that the DES N366del deletion converts the wild-type stutter into a stammer.
checks.evidence_quote: The N366del mutation converts the wild-type stutter into a different type of discontinuity, a stammer.

checks.claim: N366del mutant desmin could not form a filamentous network in 2 cell lines.
checks.evidence_quote: Expression studies in two cell lines confirm the inability of desmin molecules with this changed architecture to polymerize into a functional filamentous network.
checks.explanation: Stated for the mutants as a group, which includes N366del.

paragraphs.text: Bar et al. (2007) reported a novel c.1325C-T mutation in the tail domain of desmin, resulting in a thr442-to-ile (T442I) substitution. The mutant assembled into filaments in vitro, but filament properties differed from wild type. Coassembly with wild-type desmin severely disturbed filament formation.

checks.claim: Bar et al. (2007) reported a novel c.1325C-T mutation in the desmin tail domain resulting in a T442I substitution.
checks.evidence_quote: Here we report three novel mutations--c.1325C>T (p.T442I), c.1360C>T (p.R454W), and c.1379G>T (p.S460I)--located in desmin's non-alpha-helical carboxy-terminal "tail" domain.
checks.explanation: The variant notation is the same as in the abstract.

checks.claim: T442I mutant desmin assembled into filaments in vitro.
checks.evidence_quote: Although all but two mutants (p.E413K, p.R454W) assembled into IFs in vitro
checks.explanation: T442I is not one of the two exceptions, so it assembled into filaments.

checks.claim: Filaments formed by T442I mutant desmin had properties that differed from wild type.
checks.evidence_quote: filament properties differed significantly from wild-type desmin as revealed by viscometric assembly assays.
checks.explanation: This general statement covers the mutants that assembled, which include T442I.

checks.claim: Coassembly of T442I mutant desmin with wild-type desmin severely disturbed filament formation.
checks.evidence_quote: when coassembled with wild-type desmin, these mutants revealed a severe disturbance of filament-formation competence and filament-filament interactions
checks.explanation: This general statement about the mutants includes T442I.
